Okay, Luiza, this is a practice round. I ask, you answer right away, forty-five seconds each. Ready? Do you think students should study a topic before the class, or after it?
Before, in most cases. Although it takes time, the class makes much more sense when you already know the basic ideas.
Good start. But is there a drawback? Some students say it is overwhelming.
It can be. At my university we do it every night, and the workload is heavy. Despite that, I think the benefits outweigh the drawbacks, at least in the long run.
Nice concession. Next question. Is social media good or bad for language learners?
Honestly, it is a double-edged sword. I learned most of my English from videos, whereas my friends learned in a classroom. However, you can also spend three hours watching and learn nothing.
That example is exactly what the test wants. Last one. Would you rather cram for one big exam, or study a little every week?
A little every week, even though it is less exciting. I took it for granted in school, but when I crammed, I forgot everything in a week.
Good. You hesitated a bit on the second one. Were you torn between the two sides?
A little. But I think the trade-off is worthwhile: I lose two seconds, and I gain a better answer. How long did I take on that one?
In my opinion, students should study the topic before the class.

In the interview task you hear four questions, you have no time to prepare, and you get forty-five seconds for each answer. Most students panic in the first two seconds and try to find a perfect opinion. You do not need a perfect opinion. You need a clear one. Start with your position in one sentence. Give one reason and one real example, because examples are where your English sounds natural. Then, and this is the sentence most students forget, give the other side a moment. Say although, or even though, and accept the strongest point against you. It makes you sound mature, and it gives you ten easy seconds while you think. Finally, come back to your position, so your answer has an end and does not simply stop when the time runs out.

In many law schools, professors still use the Socratic method: they call on a student without warning and ask questions until the reasoning either holds or falls apart. Supporters say it prepares students for courtrooms, where nobody waits for you to feel ready. They also point out that students who know they may be called on actually do the reading. Critics accept that it creates discipline. However, they argue that it rewards the students who are confident, whereas quieter students, who may understand the case just as well, stay silent to avoid the risk. Some schools have found a middle ground. Instead of calling on anyone at any time, they tell a small group in advance that they will be on call that week. Despite the change, most students still say the method is stressful, but worthwhile.
